text:
Shocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027.
Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz.
But EDF’s outlook for next year currently reads: £2,254 for the second quarter, which will include about £100 extra in the “network costs” line in bills that includes paying for the upgrade of the electricity grid – demonstrating that gas prices are not the only story on a medium and long-term horizon. Then £2,078 in the quarter starting in July and £2,035 from October.
To repeat, projections can change, albeit an increasing slice of the electricity side comprises fixed costs, such as those network charges, that are nailed down in advance. The point, though, is that no one – certainly not government ministers – can claim to be surprised if this crisis lasts a while.
There are two points to make. First, the government no longer has an excuse to dodge the vexed question of a “social tariff” for energy – a scheme to give financial support to struggling households on a properly targeted basis.
The aim would be to get off today’s rickety practice of the chancellor giving 11th-hour handouts without a meaningful effort to ensure the money goes where it is most needed. This time it was £100 for council tax payers in lower bands – an inadequate proxy for poorer households or energy hardship.
The misnamed energy independence bill would give the government powers to do the necessary data-sharing work to design a proper social tariff. It’s time to hurry up with a job that has been talked about since the energy crisis of 2022 that followed Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Next winter should serve as a hard deadline to get a workable social tariff in place.
The second point is this. Even as the government under Andy Burnham has emphasised cheaper energy as a new priority, its specific target is not terribly ambitious. It is to lower UK energy costs to bring them in line with other European countries within 10 years.
The goal is more credible than Keir Starmer’s empty (or cynical) promise of “£300 off bills” in the life of this parliament. But a decade to get in line with European averages? That is not speedy. Energy costs are, by a distance, the most pressing concern for UK industry. Yes, there are discounts for a limited number of heavy users, but how is wider “re-industrialisation” meant to happen if the UK remains uncompetitive on energy for another nine years?
A more encouraging way to look at things is that the government’s emerging new thinking on energy is bolder than a 10-year timeframe would suggest. The speech at the CBI this week by Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, offered three clear lines of attack: take more costs off bills and into general taxation; accelerate electrification and grid connections and get “wasted wind” costs under control; and go after the excess profits earned not only by gas plants at moments of high system stress but also by clean power generators with revenue arrangements tied to gas prices.
All are worthwhile strategies, but in combination they ought to be capable of delivering something better than European norms sometime around 2036. If not, the Treasury’s new “cost control framework” on energy levies will have to be sweated harder.
Being charitable, one might say the loose “within 10 years” phraseology was used because every government goal at the moment is framed within Burnham’s yet-to-be-unveiled 10-year plan. One hopes so, because the war on energy costs is more urgent for businesses and households alike.
There is nothing the government can do about wholesale gas prices, of course. But the necessary transition to clean power can be pursued with far more ruthlessness on costs. The 10-year plan, when it finally arrives, should also set a few five-year targets.
digest_he:
העלייה החדה הצפויה בחשבונות האנרגיה בבריטניה מעוררת דאגה רבה, כאשר הרגולטור עשוי לקבוע תקרת מחירים גבוהה לאורך שנת 2027. על רקע זה, גוברות הקריאות לממשלה לנקוט פעולות נחרצות יותר כדי להתמודד עם משבר העלויות המעיק על משקי הבית והתעשייה כאחד.

מומחים וגורמים פוליטיים מצביעים על הצורך הדחוף ביישום תעריף חברתי ממוקד שיתמוך במשקי הבית הפגיעים ביותר, במקום מתן מענקים מאוחרים ולא מדויקים. כמו כן, נטען כי התוכנית הממשלתית לצמצם את הפער בעלויות האנרגיה מול אירופה בתוך עשור אינה מהירה דיה, ויש להאיץ את המעבר לאנרגיה ירוקה ולהפחית עלויות נלוות.
